The answer is that “decree” and “destiny” may be used here in broader or different senses. All intellectual substances may exist together in God’s knowledge: as a whole they are known simply, which is decree, and in all their detail, which is destiny. Or “intellectual substances” may mean intellects other than the First Intellect; the “world of intellects” in Tusi’s explanation may mean that First Intellect, which holds all their forms together in a simple way. The forms are one there in their simplicity, but their different natures can also be distinguished. This use of “destiny” is not the usual technical one.

It is not difficult to understand intellectual substances as being in decree or destiny, since a thing may be “in” something in different senses. Motion is in time in one sense, and time is in motion in another. Their existence in both realms at once may mean that the difference is in how they are known, not in the things known. Bodily things, by contrast, are present in decree as a whole in the world of intellects, and separately in destiny in the material world, because matter has a strong hold on them. Their detailed bodily existence is different from their unified existence in the world of intellects.

The terms may also be used in their standard senses, if we understand the eternal archetypes as part of the world of created intellects. The relation of changing things to the unchanging is timeless, so they are present in both realms together in an eternal sense. When the whole that contains all parts is considered, the separate parts have no independent status. Bodily substances, however, are considered together with their matter and are not contained in what is above them. Their detailed material existence is therefore a second kind of existence, different from their unified existence in the intellectual world.

As the author of The Judgments says, “Intellectual substances exist in decree and destiny once, because they exist only in eternity, but from two points of view: as a whole and in detail. Bodily forms and qualities exist in both realms twice: once in eternity as a whole, and once in the endless sequence of time in detail.” This may seem compressed, but the explanation is as given above. — س قده

Another way to put the argument is this: if no evil occurred in the material world—if forms never decayed or changed and never lost a later perfection—then every good would necessarily come to be and become actual. There would be no possibility of losing either an earlier or a later perfection. Matter would therefore disappear, material things would become immaterial, and every immaterial kind would exist in only one individual. The question “Why did God not create a material world without evil?” would then mean “Why did God not make do with an immaterial world, instead of creating a material world that contains evil?” The answer is that the material world contains much good. This also shows that happiness, benefit, obedience, reward, and the like could have no meaning unless misery, harm, disobedience, punishment, and their opposites were also possible. — ط مد
The answer is given by the Shaykh, Ibn Sina, in The Directives and Remarks, and later writers followed him. — س قده

I do not see a conflict here. The reports that seem to oppose this view are countered by reports like them. Nor does the verse “Few of My servants are grateful” prove the point at issue: falling short in gratitude does not mean that someone is excluded from salvation altogether. “The grateful” may mean those at the highest level, since the Arabic word is an intensive form. The small number of the grateful is also counterbalanced by the honoring phrase “My servants.” — س قده

By “perfection” here, I mean the perfection required by a kind’s nature or by an individual’s readiness. Each thing has a particular perfection proper to it: a lion’s might, for example, or a gazelle’s speed. The later perfections are not of this kind. Wisdom, for example, is not required of most people. It is not part of human nature in general, and the matter of most people is not ready for it, so lacking it is not an evil for them. In the author’s example, the straightening of the letter alif is wanted, while the curvature of the letter dal is welcome. The perfection that every member of a kind must reach is the first and second perfection, not later perfections. This reading fits the previous sentence best; the other reading fits Ibn Sina’s quotation that follows better. — س قده

This refers to explaining reward and punishment as the results of actions. There is another answer: apart from whether divine decree applies to them, the difference between voluntary actions and actions done under compulsion or necessity is self-evident. Only someone obstinate would deny it. If divine decree applying to a voluntary action made that action involuntary, it would contradict itself. In fact, decree applying to an action as voluntary confirms its voluntariness; otherwise, what was decreed would fail to occur, which is impossible in God’s decree. The author seems to confuse being subject to God’s ordering with being compelled. A voluntary act, precisely as voluntary, is subject to God’s ordering: God wills it and it necessarily occurs. He does not will the bare act while leaving out its voluntary character. — ط مد

This is what the religious teaching calls the embodiment of deeds: repeated actions give rise to settled traits, and these traits, by the permission of the all-powerful Creator, shape forms. The material of a trait and the trait itself are one; the water of existence flows through each valley according to its capacity, and light takes on the color of the glass that receives it. Traits therefore cast shadows and take forms that resemble them: the greedy trait, for example, takes the form of ants; the harmful trait, the forms of snakes and scorpions. The rest can be understood by analogy. Well said:
If a thorn has wounded you, you planted it yourself; if you wear silk, you spun its thread yourself.
The objector is Imam Fakhr al-Din al-Razi. — ط مد ظله

The charge that philosophers deny rational good and evil is a slander. How could those who are children and offspring of reason deny that reason can judge actions? The confusion comes from the objectors’ belief that philosophers define good and evil only as agreement with, or opposition to, a purpose or interest. Since they think philosophers deny purpose, they accuse them of denying good and evil too—as though they meant that a wise person should deny them.

This question has long been disputed, so it is useful to set out the main views. Philosophers, the Imamis, and the Muʿtazilites say that good and evil are known by reason; the Ashʿarites say they are known only through religious law. The Muʿtazilites themselves differ. The earliest say actions are good or evil in themselves, not because of qualities in them. Some early thinkers say that a real quality causes both goodness and badness. Abu al-Husayn holds this only for badness: goodness needs no special quality, but badness does. Al-Jubba’i says actions are not good or evil because of real qualities, but because of points of view and relations; an act can change its moral character with the circumstances, as when striking an orphan is either discipline or abuse.

To say that good and evil are rational means that reason can recognise that one action is truly praiseworthy and another blameworthy, even without a revealed law; or that reason can understand why an action is good and the law commands it, or why it is bad and the law forbids it. Not understanding the reasons for every action does not refute this view. We know in general that a wise person should not command or forbid an action that has no benefit or harm.

To say that good and evil are religious means that reason cannot know whether an action is good or bad, whether its doer deserves praise or blame, or what makes any action good or bad, either before or after revelation. Another definition says that the rational view means an action really contains a feature that makes it good or bad, whether or not reason can recognise it; the religious view denies this. On the rational view, religious law reveals and explains a goodness or badness that is already true of the action. The law cannot command an action and forbid that same action at the same time, though it can do so at different times, as when a ruling is abrogated. On the religious-only view, the law itself makes an action good or bad; it does not reveal a quality that was already there. The reversals just mentioned are possible, and there is no necessary connection between prayer and entering paradise, or between wrongfully consuming an orphan’s property and consuming fire within. On that view, God could send a faithful, devoted worshipper to hell and an unbeliever to paradise. The sounder view instead holds that a necessary connection, known by reason, links good actions to delightful forms and evil actions to painful forms. The Qur'an says, “As a reward for what you used to do,” and, “As a reward for what you used to earn”; the Prophet says, “They are only your deeds, returned to you.” So the claim that cause and effect are unrelated and that God merely acts by habit is false.

The truth is that good and evil are rational, as we know necessarily that justice and kindness deserve praise, and oppression and aggression deserve blame. Every rational person knows this, even without following a religion. Those who deny revelation, such as the Brahmins, judge this way too. Also, judging that what God commands is good and what He forbids is bad presupposes that lying is bad and that God does not lie, and that commanding what is bad or forbidding what is good is foolish and unworthy of Him. If these judgements come from reason, then reason is not shut out; if they come from revelation, the argument goes in a circle. — س قده

Since God acts with prior knowledge and approval, and no one above Him forces Him to act or competes with Him, He acts freely. The necessity philosophers speak of—“a thing does not exist until its existence is necessary”—is a necessity understood from the existence He bestows on possible effects. It is impossible to turn that into a necessity imposed on God, making Him compelled to act. — ط مد

The reply seems at first to be an argument that silences the objector, but it can be understood as a demonstration. There are two ways to make the point. First, when we ask an agent why they acted, especially if harm followed, we are asking about the compelling benefit that made the action worthwhile despite its harmful consequences. The principles and rules by which we judge our own actions are abstracted from the world’s actual order. Asking about a motive is asking about the order that made the action appropriate. Our actions follow a benefit; that benefit follows the actual order. God’s act is the actual order itself, and the benefit or wisdom we identify follows from it, as an attribute follows from what it belongs to. There is no point in asking God to make His action fit some benefit: His action is the measure of every benefit and the source from which it is understood. Nothing stands above Him to judge Him or His action.

Second, an agent is answerable for an action only when it involves something that does not belong to them. We ask about an action when it may or may not be within their control. God owns everything in every respect, so nothing He does lies outside His ownership. This does not erase good and evil, make benefit irrelevant, or allow arbitrary action. On this account, an action is good because it belongs to the agent in a way that agrees with benefit. God’s act—the existence that comes from Him—is itself beneficial, so it belongs to Him and is good in itself. To will what is good and beneficial is not arbitrary. One may still ask what the wisdom or benefit in a particular divine act is, meaning one may seek detailed knowledge of it after knowing generally that it has a benefit. But one cannot ask whether there is any benefit at all. — ط مد

It is as if someone said of those who believe in Platonic Forms that the Forms were created for what lies beneath them, their images, so that they could serve as patterns for making those images. Both objections come from misunderstanding their teaching. — س قده

The point is not that we cannot ask why because God acts from an arbitrary will. That would destroy the rational connection between things and would first of all defeat the very claim that arbitrary will makes questions of purpose impossible. — ط مد

Those who believe in eternal punishment can answer the argument by choosing either option. If a person leaves human nature and becomes a new kind through their habits, that new form is a settled trait whose true nature is attachment to matter and aversion to holiness. Once the person takes on that form and its effects appear, the soul leaves the body and the truth of the matter is revealed. The effects that follow from the soul’s own nature then cause it pain, with no way to avoid them. They are perfections that suit it, but they are painful because the person now sees what they truly are. This is like someone who has developed a harmful habit that undermines life, then learns its danger only after the habit has taken hold: while doing the act, they suffer from the very thing they enjoy.

If the person remains human in nature, the painful conditions that torment them are forced upon them, but none is everlasting or occurs for most of the time. They recur and change, as one torment interacts with another, while the soul continues along its path of misery and becomes more miserable without end. This is suggested by the verses, “Whenever its flames die down, We increase them,” and, “Whenever their skins are burned away, We replace them with other skins so that they may taste the punishment.” In short, the torment is a kind of compulsion, but the kind of torment may continue forever even though no particular torment does. The philosophers do not deny that a kind of compulsion may last forever or occur most of the time; the author himself says so when explaining why the earth is continually forced into an uneven shape, though its natural shape is a sphere. — ط مد

The answer that comes to my mind now is to choose that the person remains in the original human nature. The objector says that this nature was hidden by temporary, accidental conditions. We reply: it was hidden by settled, lasting traits and essential forms that do not pass away. The person has become like a mixture of substances such as milk and vinegar, or like an animal tied to the same post as an angel. This matter is among the secrets that most minds cannot understand, and that may harm and destroy them. It is reported that the Messenger of God once passed through a street in Medina with his companions. A woman asked them to enter her house. They saw a blazing fire, with her children playing around it. She said, “Prophet of God, is God more merciful to His servants than I am to my children?” He replied, “God is the Most Merciful of those who show mercy.” She asked, “Would you ever want me to throw my child into the fire? How, then, would God put His servants into it, when He is more merciful to them?” The narrator says that the Messenger of God wept and said, “This is how God has revealed it to me.” — س قده
This also implies that the less worthy is preferred. — س قده
The world is not one in the strict sense of having one single kind or essence; it has a kind of unity, but its parts include different kinds. — ط مد

The totality of matter and material things has no matter of its own; likewise, the totality of the world of places and things in places has no place, and the totality of times and temporal things has no time. — س قده
This is a poetic rather than demonstrative argument. — ط مد

This means the effects of the stars’ supposed unfavourable influences on particular beings in the elemental world. Saturn and Jupiter are equally fortunate in the heavens themselves, since there is no opposition or conflict among them. So there is no evil in the heavenly realm. — س قده

In interpretation, day is the light of the Real, the existence of the heavens and earth. Without the night of essences, the splendour of His face would burn away everything reached by sight, and the rays of His light would dazzle the eyes and inner vision of those who see. Indeed, there would be no one to see. If the nights of essences were endless, without the light of existence; or if the nights of bodily matter had no lights from the guiding heavenly beings and the human and animal souls that give matter life, all would remain in the deep night of nonexistence, the dark night of death and shadow. Darkness would be layered on darkness, dread on dread, terror on terror. He brings night into day and day into night, sheltering us in His mercy, giving us life by His command, and comforting us with His light. A spirit from Him is entrusted to us, and His light is a trust in our keeping; one day the trusts must be returned. If you saw the complete poverty and need of every part of the Great Human—from head to foot—you would understand the great calamity that would follow: all life, all light, all existence itself belongs to God and returns to Him. “To whom does the kingdom belong today? To God, the One, the All-Conquering.” — س قده
This agrees with the report from the Imams that such a thing cannot happen; but God must not be described as powerless. — س قده
These aches are a kind of sensory, tactile awareness. If animals were not made to feel them, they would be seriously deficient; they would have no sense of touch and no animal balance. — س قده

If this protective impulse does not occur, or does not help an individual whose body is ruined by an illness before it reaches full growth, providence does not concern itself with that rare case; the aim is universal benefit, as explained above. — س قده

You might say that neither this explanation nor what follows explains why living animals eat the bodies of other living animals. We reply that the reason is clear when we combine it with what was said earlier: the cause must be sought at the level of the whole, since the aim is common benefit and universal well-being. So the incidental urging of living animals to eat other living animals is negligible beside the protection and care given to their bodies, and the direct provision of carcasses for food. They are also given alertness, quick perception, and tools for fighting or fleeing. As the poet says: “You taught the fierce lion to attack, and gave the gazelle of Khotan its speed.” Look, people of insight, at what the wise Creator has done in this world, home to worms and a place of struggle, conflict, and change: He directs each thing toward its purpose and fulfills its true aim, as it journeys toward self-effacement in the One it worships. This is truly complete and excellent. The beauty of His work overwhelms the mind, and the precision of His ordering amazes the heart. — س قده
The relation is reversed in the world of origination: there it is active causation; in the world of creation it is receptivity. It is also a relation of sustaining what depends on another. — س قده

The plant soul continually uses its powers to grow, nourish, strengthen, and balance its own matter—its taste, smell, and other qualities—so that it can provide material for the animal soul. Likewise, the animal soul continually prepares its own matter for the human soul. Through its powers of sense and movement, it seeks what suits it and avoids what does not, preparing its matter so that it may come to your door and enter your presence. Attar points to this when he says: “The angels’ service is all for you; paradise and hell are the reflections of your kindness and severity.” — س قده

This is how things are in reality. From the longing soul’s point of view, and according to what it senses, it may seem an advantage, a perfection, or a low and harmful state. If it does not recognise what is truly sought, who is sought, and at least what manifestation or appearance is being sought, it loses out: it confines absolute light and pure beauty to the receiver, unaware of the reality and occupied with its outward form. This way of seeing gives rise to multiplicity. When reality appears and borrowed forms disappear—as God says, “The Real has come, and falsehood has vanished,” and, “When he came to it, he found it to be nothing, but found God there”—then the person is left empty-handed and cries, “Alas for what I neglected in relation to God!” — س قده

This is voluntary death, not natural death. If the wording is left unrestricted, it could include natural separation as well. The ascent of the souls that help others should be understood like sorting grain from its husks in a pile, not like sowing seeds and growing a crop. The latter kind of ascent is not possible, since this world alone is the field in which to sow: wheat yields wheat, barley yields barley. — س قده

This needs qualification. The sinful aspect of actions is privative. Every sinful act has a corresponding act of the same kind that is obedience; what distinguishes them is that one agrees with a religious or rational command and the other disobeys or abandons it. Adultery and marriage, taking another’s property by force or with consent, and killing unjustly or in lawful retaliation are examples. The disobedience and abandonment are the sinful aspect of the act, and they are absences, not existing things. This is why the Qur'an generally attributes things to creation and goodness, but attributes disobedience to evil and calls it wrongdoing: “God is the Creator of everything,” “Who perfected everything He created,” and, “How evil is the name of disobedience after faith.” Perhaps the author means that the acts described as sins exist, as the end of his argument suggests when he traces blame for gossip and adultery to disobeying a command and abandoning obedience. — ط مد

This is the meaning behind the saying: “A point moved lengthwise and became a line; the line moved sideways and became a surface; the surface moved in depth and became a body.” It is an image for what was described: the flowing point draws all things, just as the flowing instant draws time, and the middle movement draws the completed movement. Each of the three is like a spirit for what it draws. This is because everything is a sign of the Real, as the verse says: “In everything there is a sign that He is One.” Because the comparison might mislead, the author immediately adds a statement of transcendence, following the way the Qur'an joins these two claims: “Nothing is like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.” — س قده

This is the familiar proof that each immaterial kind is confined to one individual. It applies to the immaterial intellects in the descending order, but not to the other beings—such as the souls of the spheres and stars, and their bodies—because these are connected with matter. — ط مد

We discussed the Platonic Forms and this principle in Volume I. The account here of the order of creation—the souls and bodies of the spheres and stars, and their benefits and perfections—is based on the views of earlier astronomers and natural philosophers. Modern research does not confirm it. Since these detailed questions do not fall under general philosophical demonstrations, philosophy took them from related sciences as established assumptions. Now that they have been shown false or inadequate, the right course is to use the findings of modern research as assumptions and build the discussion on them. Those sciences are responsible for establishing their details. But the central claim—that the order of origination displays the most careful making and noblest arrangement—stands firm. The immaterial world reflects the divine order, the best and noblest order, and is more complete than what lies below it. The imaginal world reflects the intellectual world, which contains the fullest possible existence and noblest order, and is more complete than the material world below it. The material world—with its galaxies, suns, planets, and moons; their movements and cycles of generation and decay; its elements, their compounds, and their atoms; the fixed suns and moving planets within them; its particular systems and the universal order governing all of them according to constant principles, unchanging measures, and enduring guidance—all of this astonishes the mind with its beauty and fills the inner vision with its radiance. The wonders of creation, subtle care, and forms of good that human beings have discovered are only a drop in a vast ocean. — ط مد

The rays that descend from the sun to earth may travel in a straight line, reflect back along another line, or bend along a different line, forming an angle. Some rays fall on the waters around the earth and bend toward land. For example, when the sun is in the east, some of its rays reach the earth directly while others bend toward it, because the upper northern quarter of the earth is exposed above the water, while its lower northern quarter and both southern quarters are covered by water. — س قده

Every moving thing may fail to reach one end when considered from one point of view, yet reach an end when considered in relation to the causes and capacities that lead it there. That is the end its mover actually directs it toward. Each being turns toward one of God’s names and worships it; only the perfect human being, the greatest gate and straightest path, worships God in the fullest sense. A supposed failure to reach an end is relative to some other end that partial, imaginative minds expect, and that expectation is only imagined. A being can reach the highest end by coming to the threshold of this greatest gate. The Qur'an says, “This Qur'an guides to what is most upright,” and, “Enter houses by their doors.” + +Likewise, the claim that a human life naturally lasts one hundred and twenty years means that a natural kind is realized when at least one individual realizes it. Individuals with weaker constitutions and less balanced bodily conditions have a natural lifespan suited to their own matter and circumstances. To say they did not reach their “natural lifespan” means only that they did not reach the lifespan expected of the kind in an individual who lives longer. It is a relative and imagined comparison. The same applies to movements toward ends: expecting every individual to attain the highest end is based on the kind or class, not the individual, and is only an imagined expectation. Understand this well. — س قده

As in the saying, “Beware the insight of the believer, for he sees by God’s light.” Especially so for the person who travels through the Real and from the Real back to creation. A Persian verse says: “Look again with the pure light of the King, lest you imagine you see with a short-sighted eye.” The “angels who know” are the universal intellects; the “angels who act” are the universal souls; the powers that directly move the heavens are the imprinted souls and the celestial powers and natures. — س قده

If “preceding” means earlier in time, this would conflict with the claim that the specific forms of simple beings are created without matter and are prior to motion. The meaning must instead be either that earlier bodily forms help as receptive matter for later specific forms; that prior forms help the later forms in a timeless order, with “directions” meaning the luminous features in the lords of the kinds; or that earlier celestial forms help bring about the elements in an essential order. Some say the Active Intellect causes the four elements through the four groups of spheres. The last interpretation best fits the school of Aristotle. — س قده
The difference between this reason and the one before it is like the difference between unity and individuality in concept: unity is the broader notion. — س قده

This reason is specifically aimed at denying that there could be another individual of the same kind. If it were broadened to appeal to the unity, individuality, and knowledge of the cause, it would return to the earlier reasons. The author’s words, from “the final cause of its existence” to “the noblest possible being,” restate the point and indicate a proof without spelling it out, leaving the reader to recognise it. The explanation is that the argument seeks to establish the unity of the act, after establishing the unity of the agent and the end. If another world were proposed, it would have the same single, necessary cause; when viewed in that light, it would simply be this world, especially since we have already seen that the answer to “What is it?” is the same as the answer to “Why is it?” — س قده

You might ask how the First Intellect and the Great Human could be of one kind: the First Intellect is a separate substance in its essence and activity, while the Great Human includes the whole body, soul, and intellect. The questioner points back to the earlier claim that the two are “like each other in reality.” Given your principle that the answers to “What is it?” and “Why is it?” are one, the questioner argues that the answer to “Why does the Great Human exist?”—God—is also the answer to “What is it?” The same is true of the First Intellect. If the answer to “Why?” is the same for both, then the answer to “What?” is also the same, and they are alike in kind. — س قده

Every complete being includes the perfections of all that lies beneath it. After God, the First Intellect is the world’s form, its face and unity, and what brings it into actuality. Since it is simple reality, it must contain all the lower forms of existence in a unified way; the world is the place where that unity is unfolded into multiplicity. We have already learned that a kind is defined by its last and decisive feature, while the other defining elements prepare for it. What was first a condition becomes, in the end, a condition of completion. A thing is what it is through its form. The First Intellect is therefore the final defining feature and form of the Great Human: what makes it actual. A thing is also what it is through its completeness; what is incomplete is contained within what is complete, just as intellect is contained within the light of the Light of Lights. — س قده

Some things are gradual, such as durations, sequences, and contacts that occur at an endpoint in time. Some lie outside both classes, such as immaterial beings. Or one might say intellects are instantaneous in a timeless sense, while souls are instantaneous in their essence but gradual in their activity. Another possibility is that souls are instantaneous and intellects, which belong to the divine realm, are neither gradual nor instantaneous in a timeless sense: they remain through God, not by being continually preserved, and belong to the eternal. The first interpretation is clearest. — س قده

If you ask about the truth, every work of God is subtle and every form of nature is a wonder. But because we perceive these things gradually, we do not marvel at all of them. Also, when something exceeds a limit, it can have the opposite effect. The signs, proofs, and wonders have become so numerous that people no longer notice them. Each being, by virtue of its own nature, can do something or several things that others cannot. The complete human being alone is more wondrous than all wonders. One of our leaders is reported to have said: “The Holy Spirit in the gardens of the celestial sphere has tasted the first fruits of our gardens.” If this is the state of the Holy Spirit, what do you think the state of others is? You can see the truth of what we have said about the presence of wondrous signs if you return each existing thing to its first state: a shapeless material or an inert element, without any decoration or form. Compare that first, empty state with what has been adorned and completed by its first and later perfections, and you will see the difference between the head of a gathering beneath domes and dust, between the Lord of lords and earth. Then even the movement of the lowly earthworm becomes a wonder, and understanding it a greater wonder. The flight of a fly, which resists the air, is strange; stranger still is its care in touching its head and wings with its legs and cleaning them so they do not get dirty or weigh it down and prevent it from flying. If these things are so wondrous, what of the nobler beings—and especially the noblest being, the human being, who once passed through a time when he was nothing worth mentioning, a dirty drop and impure blood, then changed through stages into an embryo and grew until he came out of his mother’s womb, still one of the weakest creatures? He then grew to maturity and learned to distinguish guidance from error. If God’s care reaches him, he may become a person who knows God, a powerful angel, a leader who displays knowledge and power, a saint, or a prophet and God’s deputy. In the end, he gathers beings into himself, inherits them, and folds them into his own existence, just as the First Intellect is God’s deputy, giving existence to beings according to their readiness and unfolding them in their kinds at the beginning. If you are amazed, this is what is most amazing; if you are moved, this is what is most moving. So rise and sing along with the nightingale in the sanctuary of love and the songbird in the gardens of knowledge and guidance: “The unseen voice pours wine into our cup; let the musician play, for the world has gone our way. We have seen the beloved’s face reflected in the cup, though you know nothing of the pleasure of drinking without end. We delight in the eyes of our beloved; for this reason, our reins have been handed over to intoxication.” This visible human being and the wonder he displays are described in the verse of the author’s spiritual guide. — س قده

This verse strongly urges people to seek knowledge. It shows that the soul becomes fully actual and truly lives through knowledge, since every breath is in God’s hand. If people fail to reflect and die before gaining true knowledge and becoming actual through it, what teaching or inward belief could they trust to complete them after they have left the world where they could grow and become complete? The verse also shows that growth cannot continue in the next life: the next life is harvest time, while this world is the field in which it is sown. — س قده

The author means that among substances, prime matter is the weakest, and among attributes, motion is the weakest. Matter can receive all created things, and the circular motion of the heavens connects these events to the timeless First Cause. If even these two weakest things contain countless purposes and benefits, imagine what is found in stronger kinds of being. — س قده

In place of the celestial spheres described by the author, we should put the flowing nature of the whole world, divided into the simple and compound bodily kinds, whose parts are its changing movements. In place of the outermost sphere and the measure of its movement, we should put universal time, which measures this flowing nature. This follows from what was said earlier about how weak and inadequate the old theory of the spheres is. — Ismail and T. M. (editor).

Interpret “night” and “day” more broadly than their usual meanings, so that the verse includes the case where the paths of the stars coincide with the path of their shared swift movement; or take the verse as an example of what came before and what follows. — س قده

Reason judges by means of real distinctions. In nature, a universal kind either continues as one individual, as with the spheres and their stars, since individuals of a bodily kind multiply by being divided, and this cannot happen to a sphere or star; or it continues as a kind through successive individuals, as with the elements and the things made from them, which can be divided. — س قده
For this reason, when a traveling mystic was asked whether he had seen anything wondrous in his long journeys through many lands, he answered: “I have seen nothing more wondrous than myself.” — س قده

That is, the image of the meaning. The guiding spirit first takes an imaginal form, then a natural form mixed with matter. It is like pure air struck by cold until a thin cloud forms, made only from the air; then vapour enters it and makes the cloud dense. This passage refers to the spirit’s earlier state, when it was a universal intellect—or rather, in God’s knowledge—and to the soul’s priority over the body in time, being, and rank. The next phrase, “making the dense subtle,” follows the author’s established view that the soul begins through the body but endures as a spirit. — س قده

The pure, finest blood in each receptive organ takes on that organ’s nature, so in the heart it becomes something like the heart’s subtle essence. Most blood, of course, flows through the veins. Nature sends a good portion to the heart; much of it enters the heart’s right chamber and a little the left, where it becomes a vital vapour. — س قده

That is, the spirit mentioned above. Just as this vapour is the sphere of the little human world, the sphere is like the vital vapour of the great human world. This is why God calls it “smoke” in His Book. — س قده

The three layers of darkness are the darkness of the placenta, the womb, and the abdomen; or the darkness of the abdomen, the world of bodies, and prime matter. The spirit, too, has three layers of darkness: the natural form, the in-between form, and the form of the next life. It must leave all three if it is to cast off the two worlds and both sandals, even if forms are only shadows to which it pays no attention. — س قده
“What an artist, whose overflowing beauty has captured the image in its net!”

This phrase may mean that the powers are the subject of “appointed,” with the angels as the object. Or the angels may be the subject: the powers, as they face God and are connected to Him, are angels; as they face downward and connect with matter, they are powers and natures. God’s aspect is dominant over the soul’s aspect, and the powers are appointed to it. The first reading treats these two aspects as one in a certain respect. — س قده

The word may mean “or” or may be a way of moving to a new point. The number of angels cannot be counted; the reference is to the natures and spiritual powers of things both below and above. The author names one, ten, a hundred, and a thousand to suggest what was said. A similar tradition says there are one hundred and twenty-four thousand prophets. God’s words and blessings do not run out or perish, and His blessings cannot be counted. — س قده

You might say that we have no power that oversees the amounts. I think the author means the nutritive power. By “the fourth gives it the form of flesh, bone, and other things,” he may mean that the third strips away its earlier form, and that digestion is the third power. — س قده

The active principles and powers are angels insofar as they are connected to what is above them. Each higher being is like a body for the spirit above it, so every one is noble through the nobility of what is above it—indeed, radiant through the glory of God, the Praiseworthy and Glorious. They are like His seeing eyes and working hands, or levels of His active power. Since the questioner’s words suggested that a single task would be a lowly state, the author first establishes the angels’ nobility, then shows that many actions can issue from them in an ordered sequence. The universal intellects and souls—the angels brought near, who stand in rows and direct affairs—have many actions in this way. The active principles in the imaginal world do too. The powers and natures working in the hidden world have the same kind of many actions as what is above them, since a thing is what it is through its form. The questioner’s claim concerns all angels. — س قده

This is the animal power in the terminology used by doctors. It prepares the organs to receive sensation and movement. It is also the power that expands and contracts the heart and arteries, renewing the vital spirit. In short, it maintains the vital spirit. The term “animal power” is sometimes used for the brain’s powers discussed later, but that is not what is meant here. — س قده

In this terminology, an animal moves through appetite, not through will. But “will” has two meanings, one narrow and one broad. In the narrow sense, it applies to immaterial beings and refers to an intellectual inclination or something similar. In the broad sense, it applies to animals and refers to sensory and appetitive inclination. — س قده

The earth is first divided in half by the equator into northern and southern halves. A circle passing through its four northern, southern, eastern, and western points then divides it into quarters. Roughly three quarters are covered by water: the northern and southern parts below that circle, and the southern part above it. The exposed part is roughly the upper northern quarter. — س قده

The wording needs to be corrected by restoring a phrase left out of the sentence: as people travel north, the visible pole rises higher and the hidden southern pole sinks lower; the reverse happens for those traveling south. Otherwise, instead of “the reverse” the text should say “for those traveling south.” — س قده

By listing women among the animals, the author hints that women’s reason is weak, that they remain fixed on particulars, and that they desire worldly adornment, so most of their conduct is like that of animals. Yet, he says, they were given human form so that men would not be repelled by their company and would want to marry them. He uses this to explain why Islamic law gives men authority over women in many rulings, such as divorce, disobedience, and cases where harm is compounded—unlike some rulings in other religions. “How far apart are the Pleiades and the bright star!” — س قده

The animal souls meant here are those on the path toward human beings, since something is adorned by what is connected to it. The same applies to the plant souls connected to animal souls on that path, and to what lies above the rational soul, such as the divine universal soul. Separate beings are also adorned by the complete human being, who reflects them in the visible world. Natural powers reflect his nature; plants his plant life; animals his animal life; embryos and devils his capacity for cunning; working angels his practical reason, purity, and protection from sin; and angels who know his theoretical reason, wisdom, and knowledge. The sphere, which the divine Book calls “smoke,” reflects his vital spirit, form, and beauty. In short, the powers and natures of all the worlds are gathered within him in a unified way. A Persian verse says: “When we sent Adam out, we spread our beauty across the plain.”

Everything enters existence through seven things: knowledge, will, decree, measure, a record, permission, and an appointed term, as a hadith says. The “record” means its measured imaginal form. — س قده

This describes the vertical sequence of beings as they turn toward the inward realm; it does not describe events happening at particular times, since time itself is folded away. Countless moving things reach countless ends over countless periods, and all are gathered into the ultimate end. — س قده

It is easy to understand how sound might exist in the heavens, through bodies striking or touching one another as they move. As for tastes and pleasant scents, the author has hinted at how they may be there: whoever gives a perfection must possess it. Yet other beings do not receive these qualities by tasting or smelling them as we do. The clearer account is that, if God made them reach such a being, it would become a sphere—unless this were done as a miracle for a prophet. Such a being would then possess what it received, because the spheres act upon things made from the elements and have stronger active powers than fire. Another explanation, which the philosophers in Aristotle’s school would accept if they listened, is that the spheres possess these bodily perfections in a higher way, through the forms in their senses—their own inward images. These forms are present through active knowing, not passive reception, just as a human soul may create the image of a beautiful face in its shared sense even when the body it inhabits does not have a beautiful face. A scholar would judge that this person possesses the beautiful image in a higher and more complete way than the matter in which it is impressed. The ignorant person would not, because he did not see the beauty on the body. The same applies to taste, smell, and other senses. Since the spheres perceive through strong, active knowing, the author holds that their inward images are senses, as our imagination is a sense. The sphere itself, however, is simple, with similar parts, so it cannot contain different powers and natures in the way a body does. — س قده

Impure souls cannot enter heaven as particular individuals, nor can their bodies, which are unlike heavenly bodies, though the kind of human soul may be able to enter. The verse “Do not let them approach the Sacred Mosque” applies to such souls by the rule that governs their nature. — س قده

The interpretation is that holy souls belong to the higher heaven, but because they are connected to the natural world they also belong to the nearest heaven. Intellects are different: their being and attention are fully raised above it. Heaven is adorned with lamps because it is lit by knowledge, its qualities, and its actions. Among these actions are the universal divine souls, the greatest signs. Its stars drive away devils by using the light of proofs to remove doubts. — س قده

The “firm roots and branches reaching the sky” mean that the spoken word is a bounded sensory or psychic form whose effect reaches the depths of the heart and becomes a simple intellect that encompasses things. In the inward, creative word, the firm root and its other parts mean that its natural level is still while its spiritual level unfolds—or that its preserved root remains firm while its aspects spread out. — س قده

This includes the prayer during a lunar or solar eclipse and the night prayer. If the moon is near the horizon at the beginning of the night, it is high in the middle of the sky at midnight. The same applies to other nights. Many recommended prayers are set by lunar times, as those who observe them know. — س قده
This is taken from the noble traditions: the Inhabited House is truly the place where God is remembered and known. It is the station of the souls in heaven, that is, in their matter and form. — س قده

The first group are the universal intellects sought by the movements of the heavens. They are compared to the heavens. Their prostration is their complete disappearance and erasure in witnessing the transcendent Real. The second group are the universal and particular souls impressed in matter, which seek the universal intellects as manifestations of God and His overpowering lights. They bow because their existence has not vanished as completely as that of the first group; they are also directed toward the heavenly bodies. From this, a worshipper should reflect on the meanings of the postures in prayer. A Persian verse says: “Every veil He draws has a path within it.” In standing, one leaves attachment to the natural world and follows no passing desire; one rises from worldly life, stands before God, and affirms the oneness of His actions. In bowing, one lowers oneself, surrenders, and stretches out one’s neck as if ready to be struck, submitting to God’s words: “God has bought the believers’ lives in exchange for the garden”—the garden of attributes or the garden of the divine essence. The one who bows affirms the oneness of God’s attributes. In prostration, one’s existence disappears and is erased completely, affirming the oneness of God’s essence and passing away fully in Him. — س قده

That is, God formed the body and also shaped the inward soul in all forty-eight familiar forms. Some thinkers of illumination say that the body, like the soul, is impressed with the forms of things. — س قده

People are kept from this knowledge by turning away from divine philosophy and mathematical sciences, especially astronomy, the noblest of them. They know the heavens only as a color and the stars only as glints and flashes. In truth, they know nothing of the heavens: the color they see belongs to vapour and smoke. They have no understanding of what the heavens are, whether they exist, why they exist, what matter, form, and the fifth nature mean, or what their individual and universal souls are. They have shown no sign of understanding because their concerns are food, sex, and power over people in the natural world. They have not reflected on the creation of the heavens or themselves, or on their greatness, which would make worldly things seem small. They have not reflected on the lasting realm of the spirit, or how short a thousand years of bodily life is compared with the soul’s continued life—whether it is blessed and delighted by meeting God or tormented and deprived. A finite period cannot be compared with what has no end. The same is true when you compare the greatness of your holy soul with the greatness of the world: a person who has never seen a mountain thinks a camel is enormous, while someone who sees the camel beside the mountain knows how small it is.

Raise your luminous imagination to the spheres and look with astonishment at the quarter of the earth that lies uncovered by water, and at the tiny creatures crawling over it. That is how created beings look from above. Why do people cling to the earth and boast of owning it? How small it is, and how small are those who control it, compared with the vast spheres and their countless stars. Many stars are each larger than the whole earth. Look inwardly at their immense sizes, not as they appear to your outward sight—as small, dim points of light. Notice their varied movements: some travel westward against the usual order, others eastward with it; their speeds differ too. Some complete a circuit in a year, others in twelve years, others in thirty years. The slowest takes twenty-five thousand two hundred years, while the fastest completes its circuit in twenty-four hours. Others take different lengths of time. Notice how the fixed stars keep their positions in relation to one another, while the wandering stars continually change position. They are manifestations of God’s enduring life and displays of His power and care.

Then rise in your mind to the world of their individual souls, the imagination of the Great Human, whose body is the spheres and all they contain; then to their universal souls, which perceive universal and separate realities; and then to the universal intellects and overpowering lights, both those in a vertical order and those spread across one level. They are simple beings that encompass all, each a unified whole. Whoever sees them has seen God, for they belong to the divine realm. Divine qualities prevail in them, and the rules of everything other than God are consumed within them: they have no state of waiting or readiness to receive. Then follow the poet’s counsel: “O bird’s egg of possibility, you are both the white and the yolk. Spread your wings and fly beyond this old, worn sky.” Be one of those who swim in the sea of God’s greatness and stand in rows before Him, with steadiness and a firm station. The stages of completion are attachment, taking on divine qualities, and realization—or, if you prefer, a passing thought, a state, a settled trait, and a firm station. “Remain upright, as you have been commanded.” — س قده

This means the commanding lights cast upon dark beings, which are natural bodies. It draws on the noble hadith: “God created creation in darkness, then sprinkled His light upon them.” Or “His light” means existence given to beings and essences that are dark in themselves. — س قده

This refers to what the author says in Keys to the Unseen and elsewhere: every seven thousand years, the world of generation and decay is governed by one of the wandering stars, alone and in combination with the others. There are seven such periods; adding a thousand years to account for fractions and leap years in the astronomical year gives fifty thousand years, which is one of the days of the Resurrection. — س قده

The author will say that love is broader than longing: God loves Himself, and the intellects love themselves, even when they feel no longing. Longing applies only when there is a lack. The love placed in each thing preserves its being, like its first perfection; the longing placed in it seeks what it lacks, like its second perfection; and movement puts that search into action until it reaches what it seeks. In beings that can act, movement is the means by which the agent reaches its goal. It is like a necessary step toward a goal: needed to get there, but not the goal itself. — س قده

There is a question about restricting change in size to plants and animals. The philosophers also allowed a kind of interpenetration, which they counted among the movements of the heavenly spheres, even though it is not plant or animal growth. — T. M. (editor).

The first point gives every being a beloved; the second says that all existence is one reality, so that the beloved of all beings is God. Their existence is His manifestation and belongs to the same order as His. This also establishes that the cause completes its effect. Each being longs for its perfection, and its perfection belongs to the same order as itself: strong whiteness completes weak whiteness, for example, not blackness; strong light and heat complete weak light and heat, not their opposites. We have established that existence does not consist of wholly separate realities. — س قده

This may be a slip of the pen. Certainty is knowledge that something must be so and that its opposite cannot be so. It is general and lasting, and no proof can remove it. A proof may show that something which seemed certain was actually ignorance that only looked like certainty. — T. M. (editor).
A closer comparison would be an embrace mixed with playful biting and teasing between lover and beloved. — س قده

In everyday speech, “love” often means the special attachment between male and female animals: desire for sexual union. In more precise usage, it means a special attachment of a conscious being to beauty as beauty, so that the lover does not want to part from the beloved when they find them and longs for them when they are absent. All beauty, goodness, and happiness return to existence, just as their opposites return to non-existence. This kind of attachment is found between every level of existence and what is above it, between a being and itself, and between a being and the perfections that follow from it. So love must run through all beings, whether or not we say that life and awareness run through them too. This shows that love does not mean knowledge or awareness, though the two may be found together. The author’s claim that love without life or awareness is only a name may therefore need review. — T. M. (editor).

The author has proved that knowledge goes with existence apart from matter. Matter, and material things such as bodies, cannot be present to themselves in this way, so they are not directly knowing subjects or objects of knowledge. For knowledge to run through all beings and for bodies to be called knowing means that their imaginal and intellectual forms—their actual perfections—know themselves and other things. Knowing them means knowing them through their imaginal and intellectual forms. The same account applies to power: active power means that something can produce effects. In material things, this means that their imaginal and intellectual forms are the sources of their effects, since bodily power is only the possibility of acting, not its full activity. If knowledge and power run through all beings, so does life, which means that a being can know and act. — T. M. (editor).

The wording would be clearer as “its different kinds come to be through forms,” which is probably how the original read. If “it becomes kinds” is retained, then if this means bodily forms, these are general kinds arranged in levels; if it means species-forms, these are specific kinds at the same level. In either case matter becomes different kinds through forms. — س قده
The forms of the four elements and the heavenly sphere; the number becomes six when we include the specific form found in compound things. — س قده

When the subject changes and disappears, its accidents follow it into non-existence, while their opposites take their place. Logicians call this an “opposite” whether or not it exists as a thing. The author may instead mean an opposite in the terminology of the philosophers; this follows from the fact that an accident ceases to exist when its subject does, since the subject is one of the things that make it what it is. — س قده
